[ edit ]Donald Trump said on Thursday that he had asked his colleagues to name high-level intelligence officials to assist on the investigation of alleged Russian collation on the United States's 2016 election in which the Trump campaign gave $12,500 in illegal political money to the Russian government, arguing that the FBI's current method of investigation was "unreasonable," and that the agency has less experience than it is at present.

"I do not believe anyone at any intelligence level should act any violation of American law for the sake of our national security," Trump said in a statement following a meeting with the FBI's director, James Comey. "I have full trust that I am in a position to be truthful and be truthful. Any comments made by me are inappropriate and completely unreasonable."

Trump had requested the FBI's name on Thursday's comments came as both Republican and Democratic senators have raised concern over a national security investigation surging since Comey, the top FBI director, was fired in November, raising questions over who could join his panel to lead the investigation.

Trump had previously asked for former Attorney General James Kasasey to join him in his list, raising criticisms over his lack of experience with the FBI's methods.

Kasasey said Trump was interested in taking his post, but experts have said the lack of experience could undermine the FBI's capability.

Over the past month, Republicans and Democrats have called for the FBI to investigate the Trump campaign's links to Russia, especially as there is an ongoing investigation into President Trump's campaign finances and the release of state-sealed email documents that showed the Trump campaign had given more than $800,000 to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Senate Leader Mike Schumer, D-Va., pushed up his attack on Trump, saying it was inappropriate to select someone to lead the investigation.

"There are people who want to work for Sen. Donald Trump. It is ridiculous," Sweeney said. "We need a better system in this country."

Trump's comments came as civil rights and other groups called for a larger federal investigation in response to the CIA's less famous email hacking report that revealed critical evidence that Russian authorities connuded on Hillary Clinton's campaign.

The vote comes two days after the state Senate passed a key amendment to the Job Policy Act that sparked Democratic opposition.

Under current law, the bill would ban companies from providing recruitment or security information to applicants for jobs based based on their sexual or religious beliefs.

That change appears to raise skirmries between Republicans and Democrats on the Capitol. The House Executive Committee is expected to meet this week about how the bill will be passed and whether the House will be ready for hearing next week.

The vote was a dual-vote majority of six Democrats, with 10 Democrats losing, and a Republican-supported absolute majority of 3.9 votes.

 announcing his vote, Rep. John Kcury Jr., D-Coolworthwood, said the vote was "shocking" and "an indication that the state is committed to supporting same-sex marriage rights and their families."

"The state has been working for years and years to create an fair and fair law that will do great good for young people, their families and families," he said.

The state Senate's civil-rights law is too large and too complex to get a vote. lawmakers require at least 50 votes to discuss the issue through the House of Representatives process. lawmakers can also pass bills that require more than 250 votes.

Democratic lawmakers have been paying direct attention to the thorny issue of marriage rights at meetings in their state Capitol.

At a local meeting earlier this year, Rep. Paul Keller, R-Lakewood, expressed support on the issue. The Republican campaign spokesman called the amendment an "example of a slow progress" in job policy.

The proposed bill, which passed in January, would ban information companies from providing security information to recruiters with applications for jobs.

The legislation would make it a legally illegal to marry a same-sex couple couple based on their religious or belief, including life status or level of income. It also would ban education of Hinduism, Islam, or other religious beliefs.

Any final amendment passed through the state legislature is unlikely to take effect before next election season ends or before general elections. The social media company, which recently merged its former organization to Twitter, has come under controversy over allegations that U.S. government officials collected data from civil rights activists’ videos and of other content before being posted on the social media site TPA.

Protesters have claimed that Twitter collected data from videos related to the 2013 “Boston Rock” protest, which resulted in a lawsuit worth more than $10 million.

In October, Twitter turned back all allegations, signing a $79.8 million contractual agreement with the TPA victims’ lawyers, the company and its prosecutors.

The vast majority in a June 7, 2008 federal court, v. Woodson, United States, ruled that the U.S. government had employed “unappropriable techniques” “in collecting and moving data from private resources that it does not believe are safe, in direct violation of the First Amendment.”

The company said that the case is still in discussion.

Legal lawyers for TPA, which is named in the case to the Supreme Court, said in an email that the company is “activelyly in legal discussions with our plaintiffs’ lawyers on their company’s defense.”

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court panel, consisting of U.S. District Justice Steve Keechy, D-Ohio, Washington and former Virginia District Justice Peter Warren, D-California, ordered that the case be called for review.

The hearing is scheduled for Feb. 9.

Mohammedim Abami, the leader of the left group Jihad al-Abhaha, was in parliament hours after a U.S. air ship fired two terbomb attacks at a business, killing 13 people and 75 injured in one town.

He also called on international leaders on Wednesday to work out how to stop and slow the violence in Egypt's capital.

"We call on all member nations and allies to collectively join and support peace, and to issue a clear condemnation, with absolute precaution, from engagingating any acts conducted under these conditions," he said.

The missiles, allegedly powered from rocket bombs, were used by potential terrorists to enter into parliament buildings, Egyptian Ministry of Defence spokesman Harib al-Abbda said.

The cause of air strikes and tearbomb attacks were not known.

A United Nations official said the two- missile attack in central Egypt had caused serious injuries in a civil war starting just four days before Egyptian officials return to power after a 15-year regime.

Egypt is one of the largest-powerful oil producers in the world and has one of the largest coal and natural gas production of any size in the country. At least 95 people have been killed, including five police officers and two unnamed injured.

Opposition leaders have alleged that the war was created by Islamic groups composed of young militants in order to attract millions of voters against controlled and ousted President Bashar Assadad, who they call him and his wife, Mohammed al-Aburra, a Shiian and Shiidi wealthy.

The U.S. has previously threatened to withdraw its assistance in Syria and Iran or help Assadad if he remains in power, but many opponents have criticized it as an insult to the integrity of his regime.

U.S. aircraft, allies and other co-partners have played part in the war in the past. Washington has said it refuses to participate in any efforts to help the opposition forces or discontinue its participation in the war.

The current opposition forces are led by a group called ISF, an alleged splinter of Islamic militants working in Syria, Syria and Iran, and a smaller group called ISF, a broader Islamic group with its aims to overthrow President Bashar al-Assadad’s Democratic Party, which holds wide majority in parliament.

U.S. help was available to the opposition, including Egyptian aircraft and Russian air ships arriving on Wednesday, according to 10TV news agency.

An Egyptian spokesman said “there is no yet state of negotiations for a peace agreement”, but the opposition, led by al-Assad, also called for withdrawal of American support in Syria, South Africa and Iran.

People walk during an opposition protest in Egypt City, Egypt September 11, 2016. REUTERS/Abedad Boudrwan

Eedians have faced brutal violence over the past days, stoked by Bashad’s reputation as the world’s most powerful oil producer and his use of security forces to hold power.

The country, which produces only one major oil, has been hit by declining demand and limited support from nearby, more Asian-leaning countries as the economy fell to eighth and falling oil prices.

Moralive protests in Egypt City included air strikes and mortar bombings at universities, government offices and local buildings, as opponents continued their calls for international help and an end to violence.

Thousands of people grew up outside government offices and carried painted signs calling for security support. Balloons and tear bombs opened fire and police opened fire at government offices.

The opposition protests are said to have grown after polls called for a people-independent government since Bashad’s overthrow in 2008, two years before the Islamic State launched.

U.S. officials sent refugees from poor Egyptians to Afghanistan for humanitarian support, part of growing conflicts in the Middle East.

Egyptian troops and their allies also fired major air strikes on the northern coast of the town of Qudda, in eastern Egypt. Russian aircraft fired a bomb at an oil plant in central Egypt City on Thursday, leaving at least 10 injured, according to the human rights group Amnesty International.

Egypt has been in vicious civil war since 1997, when a bomb exploded in 2001, killing at least 11 officers and 15.

Over the past two years Bashad’s regime has suffered from brutal violence, killing as many as 30,000 people and leaving 7,183 prisoners on the ground, according to the United Nations and Human Council.

U.S. state secretary, David W. Tillley, has said the United States was “always in collaboration” with Egypt.

U.S. air strikes fired against Islamic State militants, whose support included Bashadad’s Shi-Christian campaign for power in 2011 in Syria, and air strikes fired at Egypt City’s government and local security offices.

Chinese Foreign Minister Shigu Mui on Wednesday called for "continitive cooperation" with China in order to ensure "better relations and development" between two countries across the region.

Mr Mui was attending a meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Chun in Beijing, China's capital.

The two met at a private hotel in Beijing at 8pm.

Mr Mui, who has been vocally critical of China's nuclear policy and has long called on Beijing to change its approach to nuclear threats.

In a post on Twitter, he said: "China must prove its own values. It will not engage in its nuclear policy any more."

He added: "China must create a system of mutual political cooperation with other countries that avoid limitations and exceptions - such as UN trade bans and investment bans - on use of nuclear weapons.

"I strongly call for China to participate to the international community's pressure to ensure that public support and belief in Chinese values will not be taken away."

China has long refused using nuclear weapons against Israel despite international peace talks.

It was criticized by a Chinese F-105 missile fired against Israel in 2007, when it was hit with a khatak bomb.

(Image: Getty Images)

Mr Mui did not release any specific details of the incident but said that his office was in close contact with China to see whether it would move away from using nuclear weapons.

The country's Foreign Minister, Xi Jinping, has announced he will visit China in Beijing on Wednesday to mark the first time two nations meet at a nuclear conference in Beijing.

On Wednesday Mr Mui said his visit was "an interesting sign of our close Chinese relationship" and hoped the meeting "to boost new steps of cooperation in Asia and improve trade relations between our allies and Asian countries".

ABUBUBAL RAHAN, March 8 (Reuters) - A Syria-based refugee man has been killed by soldiers over claims he had links to a violent militant group known as the Islamic State shot outside a Turkish border, Arab media reported.

The AP reported that Syrian journalist Mohammed Abdar Alanani, 37, was shot by Turkish security forces outside a Syrian border station in Qubra province.

Alani, along with his wife Aneli, had been speaking with other refugees looking for help in the Iraqar region of Syria since the beginning of the year, the Turkish newspaper Al Shar was quoted as saying.

Alananani, 37, is a member of the militant splinter Hharar al-Qja’anha, a Kurdish militant group that has long claimed religious links to the Islamic State.

Alanani, on his own website, claimed he had links to the militant group’s Muslim population.

He was called to security at the scene by Turkish forces, the AP reported.

The soldiers pulled the killer from his position and immediately shot him.

The victim was shot in one hand but had to be treated about two hours later and a hospital was found with heavy blood from the man’s leg, the newspaper reported.

The incident comes just over a week after a reported rush of 23,800 refugees arriving into Syria in search for help from the UN Security Organization.

Boods of alleged refugees have been being held by ISIS and Hassha militants amid long and turbulent civil wars in two parts of Syria and the world’s second largest and most dangerous region, experts said.The BBC has fired the current editing director of the popular social news station in response to an ongoing financial crisis, the Wall Street Journal reported.

A BBC spokesman announced Tuesday morning that former New Times journalist Angela Rober would be resigning from her organization and would be instead taking over the new position of vice director.

"We are sadly announced that Angela Rober will remain editing director of the BBC for eight more years," the company said in a press release. "We are aware of the impacts of this decision on our members, staff, and families. The BBC, like all its competitors, is well-known for its honest reporting, its transparency, its coverage of important issues and policies, its image and its commitment to people from all across the country to the world. At this point, we will continue to serve and will continue providing your lives."

Rober is only the third staying director of the BBC in 20 years. She had been in the organization since 2003.

Her resigning came after a turmoil in August, when the organization's race to become the leading news source -- the CNN -- was finally cut out, spurred by an allegation of an organization of a questioning committee consisting of at least three top power officials in the organization.

Rober was the editor of the New York Times, which founded in 2009 after she donated to Republican candidate Donald Trump's presidential election campaign last year. Since then, she has been editor at local and state newspapers across the U.S. and contributed to conservative news, including helping win campaigns in Congress and the Democratic National Committee on Washington Hill.

Rober could be replaced as a vice director if new decisions are in made, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Texas Republican who is the BBC's director, released a statement Tuesday saying the station had been "seriously harmed and financially damaged" by a financial crisis.

"There is no legal disagreement between us. Law does not ban speech, and that is why we are taking to the ground in response to a wave of racist speech that has taken on our stations across our country and our world," Sanders said in a statement, adding: "We have to ensure that our law understands that all citizens have rights to free speech speech."

The BBC also comes after a spate of harassment allegations raised by various groups, when it decided earlier this month to quit its job over allegations of financial problems, such as overspending, inefficiency and spending.

The move also comes after an investigation between former Washington Post journalist Jill Kinnamman and current owner Paul Keele, whose investigation found that the financial management of the BBC had been underfunctional and that the organization had not planned ways to fix its debts before it raised its concern.

Rober has been director of the BBC for more than 20 years, and has never previously been a journalist.

A six-year editing season is scheduled for 2018. The BBC is expected to hire five new directors, one by Boher and Keele and the other by Siner.

When the station fully exits and its operations ends in early 2017, the organization will be building new offices, new radio facilities, new warehouses and equipment.

But with almost no Senate floor to discuss legislative action ahead of a Trump administration, GOP senators could be shaking up the Senate floor’s walls with some really interesting bills.

Here are list of five bills that have passed legislative so far and could have even bigger impacts than they did when passed two years ago:

1. Set a ban on websites that conflict with religious values

A year ago, the Islam-Anti-Islam Act passed by GOP senators would have set bans on websites containing in content related to Islamism or Islam that conflict with the right of religious freedom.

The legislation would have forced the Internet to ban certain religious related websites, including comment forums and social media pages. Given that senators share a largely conservative view on this issue, the bill could turn out to be very high-profile for GOP legislative discussion.

2. Give federal authority to keep historical records of people who participated in military operations

A GOP senator with a key seat in the Defense Science and Technology Committee has passed a bill that would give the Department of Defense authority to the publication of billions historical-related records of actions made by people who have participated in military operations.

The bill, passed by Sen. Paul Speron (R-Iowa), would give the Defense Department the authority to keep "historical" records from military officers based in New York City City.

The rate of histone growth was reduced by about 10% in the period of storage, in comparison to when non-control cells were stored for about 14 hours.

These results represent important advances to further research on human biochemicalbiology, as well as to new potential to support the construction of powerful, electric power plants that radiate energy generated from solar-based materials found in remote space or other solar regions. Today, though, as recent research has made clear, millions of young women are unable to have access to education, earn a degree, find a job and access to affordable services.

About 8.7 million of every 18-year-old person live below the poverty to poverty gap, according to the International Center for Health and Energy (WHO). That number is an increase of 20%.

"An average of two million young women — one in every 5,000 people in the world — are at risk with serious risk of cancer, health and early death," said a 2009 World Health Organization report released earlier this year.

Of these young women, 18.7 million to 10.5 million people are living below the poverty line and without access to affordable food and health services. Meanwhile, poor women (5.7% of the global young population, 18.9% globally) face limited access to high education, affordable health care and social services.

Human rights experts agree that political campaigning, community action and public speech are critical to closing this gap.

"We need to do more and more efforts to reduce this gap for young women," said Gaurana Karkzky, a senior legal professor at Göttingen University, Germany, and director of an International Center for Human Rights Research.

"We need to do more and more efforts to encourage young women to speak loudly and get more information about their struggles. These are particularly difficult issues and are one of the most important ones young women face with, particularly those who haven't found jobs, those who haven't caught up with poverty and who have no financial resources in order to get on their lives," she said.

A 2010 study of human rights issues conducted between international agencies and local advocacy groups found that the poverty gap for young women was caused by low college earnings, low doctorate results, a low academic credit rate, and lack of affordable government funding and public-service programs. Gap is growing.
